newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ortega warns of deepening crisis in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Ortega warns of deepening crisis in Nicaragua.

text.p: Sandinista Front leader Daniel Ortega warned on Sunday of a deepening post-election crisis in Nicaragua if election authorities do not address the controversy left by a divisive vote his party has charged was fraudulent.

The Oct. 20 presidential election was apparently won by right-winger Arnoldo Aleman 51 percent to 37.7 percent, but Ortega has refused to concede defeat. He has charged that the elections were riddled with irregularities and fraud.
Nicaragua's Supreme Election Council (CSE) will rule by Nov. 20 on a Sandinista legal appeal for new elections in two populous provinces.

"If the Supreme Election Council maintains things the way they are, the crisis is going to deepen. We are now in a crisis and it will deepen. A lot depends on the attitude of the next government," Ortega told Reuters in an interview.

The elections, and the Sandinista rebellion against them, have created a deep split in society, as boisterous Sandinista activists resent what they see as a theft of the election by Aleman's Liberal Alliance.

Ortega has said he will respect the "legality" but not the "legitimacy" of a future Aleman government -- raising the specter of political disorder, since the Sandinistas have 40 percent of the seats in the National Assembly and a hefty bloc of city councils as well as legions of street protesters.
"This electoral process, how it unfolded, is leaving deep wounds on Nicaraguan society and a great fracture in the democratic process," Ortega said.

He said he had heard rumours of the formation of armed leftwing groups to defend the social reforms implemented by the 1979-1990 left-wing Sandinista government, but had no more information on them and did not support their formation.
"In a context like this, where the people are starting to mobilise out of concern, spaces are opened for protest. Sometimes even violent protest," he said.
International and national observers have described Nicaragua's elections as flawed but fair, and have discounted allegations of widespread fraud.
